clue.text: It brings luck for first of May race meeting

indicators.note: first of tells us to take only the opening letter of the word May

parts.note: Ascot is the famous royal race meeting held at the Berkshire racecourse

explanation.surface: A lucky charm is recommended for a horse-racing day in May.
explanation.walkthrough: ASCOT is a racecourse near Windsor whose June meeting is a fixture of the English social season.
explanation.definitionFit: A mascot is a person, animal or object kept as a token of good fortune.

clue.text: As in rate revision? Well, this describes it

indicators.note: a revision reworks something, so the letters of these three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A puzzled query about rewriting a rate, followed by a shrug of 'Well'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' looks like a conversational filler; it is the noun the answer describes, as in an artesian well, which gushes under its own pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: Artesian is the adjective for a bore-hole where water rises unaided by pumping.

clue.text: Member of the army, or of a body

explanation.surface: Two kinds of membership: a soldier's rank, or belonging to a physical frame.
explanation.definitionFit: A corporal is a junior non-commissioned officer in an army; as an adjective the word means relating to the human body.

clue.text: Its growth in N America surpasses Amsterdam's noted export

definitions.text: Its growth in N America surpasses Amsterdam's noted export

parts.words: Its growth in N America surpasses Amsterdam's noted export
parts.note: a North American plant named after Holland's famous bulb flower, but growing far taller than any bulb, into a full forest giant

explanation.surface: A horticultural boast that an American plant outgrows Dutch flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: Amsterdam's noted export is the tulip; the tree that shares its name grows to great height in the eastern USA.
explanation.definitionFit: The American tulip tree, Liriodendron, is a tall hardwood whose flowers resemble the bulb's blooms.

clue.text: Might such love of philosophy buck up the port authority ?

parts.note: PLA is the Port of London Authority
a tonic is something that bucks you up or revives you

explanation.surface: A question whether a philosopher's affection could cheer up harbour officials.
explanation.walkthrough: The PLA (Port of London Authority) runs the tidal Thames; a tonic for it comes after it in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Platonic love, named after Plato's philosophy, is affection free of physical desire.

clue.text: Divine enters tall building on river to seek concealment in Dorset

indicators.note: enters says the Divine's letters go into the building's letters

parts.note: a pile is a large imposing building
DD is Doctor of Divinity, so a divine is a DD
the Trent is a major English river
to hide is to seek concealment

explanation.surface: A clergyman goes into a tower beside a river to lie low in the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: DORSET is a county in south-west England; this village takes its name from the River Piddle, and TRENT is the Midlands river.
explanation.definitionFit: Piddletrenthide is a village in the Piddle valley of that south-west English county.

clue.text: Job too good for Walker ?

parts.note: a horse or runner that goes at a brisk gait is too fast to count as a mere walker; the clue reads like a career grumble

explanation.surface: Someone named Walker is told a post is beyond them.
explanation.walkthrough: Walker looks like a surname; read it as one who walks, outpaced by one who trots.
explanation.definitionFit: A trotter is a horse bred and trained to race at a trot, quicker than walking pace.

clue.text: State banks are ruined

indicators.note: ruined says the letters of banks and are are wrecked and rebuilt

parts.note: used as anagram fodder together with are

explanation.surface: A financial disaster: a state's banks have collapsed.
explanation.definitionFit: Nebraska is one of the United States, on the Great Plains.

clue.text: Classic hero keeps American Indian imprisoned

indicators.note: imprisoned says the letters sit locked up inside the run of words before it

explanation.surface: A classical hero holds a Native American captive.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cherokee are a Native American people originally of the south-eastern United States.

clue.text: Alarmed by organization of LSD treat

indicators.note: organization arranges things, so the letters of the following words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is frightened by a drug party being set up.
explanation.definitionFit: Startled means suddenly frightened or surprised.

clue.text: Bristol Channel — swimmer lost his toes

definitions.text: Bristol Channel — swimmer lost his toes

parts.words: Bristol Channel — swimmer lost his toes
parts.note: Edward Lear's nonsense poem tells of a toeless creature who swam the Bristol Channel and lost his toes on the way

explanation.surface: A news report of a cross-channel swimmer's grim injury.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bristol Channel is the sea inlet between Wales and south-west England; Lear's poem is 'The Pobble Who Has No Toes'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pobble is the title creature in Edward Lear's poem, whose toes vanished during that swim.

clue.text: Bar is in evidence in court

definitions.text: Bar is in evidence in court

parts.words: Bar is in evidence in court
parts.note: a legal rule that stops a party from asserting in court something contrary to what they previously said or did

explanation.surface: The barristers are visibly present in the courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: Bar suggests the barristers; here it is a bar in the sense of a legal impediment.
explanation.definitionFit: Estoppel is a doctrine of law that prevents someone from denying facts they have earlier asserted.

clue.text: Greek geographer returns nothing to London hospital

indicators.note: returns means the hospital's name is read back to front

parts.note: Barts is St Bartholomew's Hospital in London
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: An ancient scholar comes back empty-handed to a London hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: St Bartholomew's, London's oldest hospital, is universally known as Barts; 'returns' acts on its name alone, with the zero tacked on afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Strabo was a Greek scholar of the first century BC who wrote the Geographica.

clue.text: A commoner's address taken by one Russian ruler in India

parts.note: Mr is the form of address for an untitled man
I is the Roman numeral for one
a tsar was the emperor of Russia

explanation.surface: A man's address is taken over by a Russian emperor in India.
explanation.definitionFit: Amritsar is a city in the Punjab, home of the Golden Temple.

clue.text: A roguish doctrine that's anti-government

parts.note: a political creed opposed to all rule by the state, painted as the outlook of rebels and rogues

explanation.surface: A description of a lawless political belief.
explanation.definitionFit: Anarchism is the political theory that all government should be abolished.

clue.text: Indigo, if the Italian version

parts.note: an is an archaic word for if, as in Shakespeare's 'an it please you'
il is the Italian for the

explanation.surface: Asking whether the colour indigo has an Italian name.
explanation.definitionFit: Anil is the West Indian shrub that yields indigo dye, and the dye itself.

clue.text: Lexicographer's number one beast

parts.note: the animal that comes first in an English dictionary's alphabetical listing

explanation.surface: A dictionary-maker's favourite animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'number one' suggests a favourite; it means first entry alphabetically.
explanation.definitionFit: The aardvark, an African burrowing anteater, is traditionally the first word in a dictionary.

clue.text: " Methinks I am a prophet new- "(Richard It)

definitions.text: " Methinks I am a prophet new- "(Richard It)

parts.words: " Methinks I am a prophet new- "(Richard It)
parts.note: John of Gaunt's line in Shakespeare's Richard II, completed by the missing word meaning given divine insight

explanation.surface: A quotation with a gap from Shakespeare's history play.
explanation.walkthrough: Gaunt says 'Methinks I am a prophet new inspired' before his 'This England' speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspired here means filled with divine guidance, as a prophet is.

clue.text: Cat i' the adage let "I not " wait upon "I would "

definitions.text: Cat i' the adage let "I not " wait upon "I would "

parts.words: Cat i' the adage let "I not " wait upon "I would "
parts.note: Lady Macbeth's taunt in Macbeth, comparing her husband to the cat in the proverb who wanted fish but would not wet its feet; the missing verb means to venture

explanation.surface: A misquoted line from Macbeth with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is 'Letting I dare not wait upon I would, Like the poor cat i' the adage'.
explanation.definitionFit: To dare is to have the courage to venture something, which the hesitant cat lacks.

clue.text: Joys of French cat's-meat

parts.note: de is French for of
lights are animal lungs, traditionally sold as cat's meat

explanation.surface: The pleasures of French pet food.
explanation.walkthrough: Lights, the lungs of slaughtered animals, were sold by British cat's-meat men as pet food.
explanation.definitionFit: Delights are great pleasures or sources of joy.

clue.text: Rees, going round circuits of 19 course, falls back

indicators.note: going round says the name surrounds the circuits

parts.note: taken as written
laps are circuits of a racecourse

explanation.surface: A runner called Rees drops back while doing laps of the course.
explanation.definitionFit: Relapses means slips back into a former, worse state.

clue.text: Drink to a Social Security pioneer, say

indicators.note: say signals that we want a word that sounds like the pioneer's name

parts.note: William Beveridge wrote the 1942 report that founded the British welfare state

explanation.surface: Raising a glass in honour of the founder of social security.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Beveridge's report laid the foundations of Britain's post-war welfare state.
explanation.definitionFit: A beverage is any drinkable liquid.

clue.text: Grub up-bachelor tucked in — then 'e played Hamlet

indicators.note: tucked in places the bachelor's letters inside the reversed grub
in a down clue, up says the word is written from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
BA is a Bachelor of Arts
'e is a dropped-h he, giving the letter E

explanation.surface: A Cockney account: dig up a single man, then he played Shakespeare's prince.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up' reads the larva word from the bottom; 'tucked in' nests the degree in it. The dropped h of 'e mimics Cockney speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Burbage was the Elizabethan actor who first took the role of Shakespeare's Danish prince.

clue.text: Go for record in a Devon river

indicators.note: in places the record inside the river

parts.note: the Dart flows through Devon to Dartmouth
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: Going to fetch a record that fell in a West Country river.
explanation.definitionFit: To depart is to leave or set off.

clue.text: Such bombing needs savoir faire, I state

parts.note: tact is social savoir-faire, knowing how to behave
Cal is an abbreviation of California

explanation.surface: Someone claiming that a particular air attack demands social grace.
explanation.definitionFit: Tactical bombing supports immediate battlefield aims rather than strategic ones.

clue.text: English pope needs a doctor-in a lot of trouble

indicators.note: trouble means disorder, so the letters before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: An English pope is in serious trouble and needs medical help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lot of trouble' rearranges IN A into IAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Adrian IV, born Nicholas Breakspear, was the only Englishman to be pope.

clue.text: .Begorra, what a bull !

explanation.surface: An Irish exclamation of amazement at a large animal.
explanation.walkthrough: An Irish bull is a self-contradictory statement, here not an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Begorra is a stage-Irish exclamation, a turn of speech typical of the country; an Irish bull is a ludicrously illogical remark, also called by this name.

clue.text: Terrible reek round the border, of course

indicators.note: round places the scrambled smell around the border
terrible says the smell's letters are mangled

parts.note: an edge is a border

explanation.surface: A dreadful smell at the frontier, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads as 'naturally', but the definition is the course of a meal; 'Terrible' scrambles the smell and 'round' wraps it about the border.
explanation.definitionFit: Kedgeree is a dish of rice, fish and eggs, served as a meal's course.

clue.text: One of nine is inside for improper handling

indicators.note: inside says the second word goes within the first

parts.note: the Muses were the nine goddesses of the arts
taken as written

explanation.surface: One of the nine goddesses is indoors, accused of mishandling something.
explanation.definitionFit: Misuse is wrong or improper use of something.
